beats.intro: Chapter five, lesson one. Big molecules, built from small ones. [[meal]]Take a bowl of pasta, or a slice of bread. [[cell]]It is food made of cells, and cells are made of molecules. [[chain]]And the biggest of those molecules are all put together by the same simple trick.
beats.classes: Living things contain four classes of large biological molecules. [[carb]]Carbohydrates. [[lip]]Lipids. [[prot]]Proteins. [[nuc]]And nucleic acids. [[big]]Each one is a macromolecule, thousands of atoms joined by covalent bonds. [[fit]]And in all of them, structure and function go together. The shape decides what the molecule can do.
beats.poly: Three of these four classes are built the same way. [[unit]]Think of a paper clip. One small building block is called a monomer. [[long]]Join many similar blocks end to end, and the chain is a polymer. [[three]]Carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids are polymers. [[lipid]]Lipids are not. They are large, but they are not chains of repeating units.
beats.examples: Here are three real polymers. [[starch]]Starch, the energy store in pasta and bread, is a carbohydrate. Its monomer is a sugar called glucose, and one starch chain strings thousands of glucose units together. [[protein]]A protein is a chain of amino acids. Cells use twenty kinds, and a protein may link hundreds of them. [[dna]]And DNA, a nucleic acid, is a chain of nucleotides, which the next lessons open up. [[table]]Three classes, three kinds of monomer, and one way of joining them.
beats.lipids: So why are lipids left out? [[fat]]A fat, like the oil in a pan, is built from a few small pieces: one glycerol backbone and three fatty acid tails. [[few]]That is a handful of parts of different kinds, not a long chain of the same repeating unit. [[water]]What lipids share is that they mostly avoid water, and that is how they are grouped, not by a repeating pattern. [[none]]Large and important, but not a polymer.
beats.q3: Quick check. Match monomer to polymer.
beats.dehy: How does a cell add a block to the chain? [[ends]]Each monomer has an H at one end, and an O H at the other. [[meet]]Bring a new monomer to the end of the chain. [[lose]]The chain gives up its H, the monomer gives up its O H, and together they leave as one molecule of water. [[bond]]The two blocks are now joined by a new bond. That is a dehydration reaction: water removed, bond formed, polymer longer. [[again]]Repeat it, and the chain grows one block at a time.
beats.enz: Left alone, this would be far too slow. [[enz]]Enzymes are macromolecules that speed it up. [[grab]]An enzyme holds the two blocks in just the right position. [[snap]]The bond forms, the water leaves, and the enzyme is free to work again.
beats.hydro: Breaking a polymer is the reverse. [[water]]A water molecule comes in. [[split]]It splits. Its H goes to one block, and its O H goes to the other, and the bond between them breaks. [[name]]This is hydrolysis: water added, bond broken, polymer shorter. [[eat]]It is what happens when you digest your food. Enzymes in your gut chop big polymers back into monomers small enough to use.
beats.worked: Let's count with a bigger chain. [[ten]]Build a chain of ten glucose units. [[bonds]]Ten units in a row have nine links between them, so nine bonds. [[waters]]Each bond forms by dehydration, and each dehydration releases one water. So building the chain releases nine water molecules. [[back]]Now digest it fully. The same nine bonds break, each hydrolysis uses one water, so nine water molecules are added, and ten glucose units come out. [[rule]]The rule: for n units, there are n minus one bonds, and n minus one water molecules, either way.
beats.diverse: Now, variety. [[cells]]A single cell holds thousands of different macromolecules. [[vary]]They differ between the cells of one body, differ more between members of a species, and differ even more between species. [[letters]]Yet they all come from a small set of monomers. Twenty-six letters spell every word in a library. [[order]]The same blocks, in a different order and length, make a different polymer.
beats.q2: Quick check. Why so many polymers?
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Four classes of large molecules. Three are polymers, built from monomers. [[w2]]Dehydration removes water and forms a bond. Enzymes speed it up. [[w3]]Hydrolysis adds water and breaks a bond. [[w4]]A small set of monomers, in different orders, gives endless variety. [[end]]Now try the chapter practice.
